# hexvero

> hexvero is an Electron release diff for security review: it compares two builds of an Electron app (app.asar, .app bundle, install directory or release ZIP) and reports what changed in IPC channels, contextBridge members, window settings, network hosts and storage, with the file and line on both sides, plus a release policy check for CI. It is an open-source (MIT) command-line tool, MCP server and local web UI for static, execution-free analysis of software artifacts: native binaries (ELF, PE, Mach-O), Electron and JavaScript apps, Android APKs, .NET assemblies, WebAssembly, SQLite databases and more. It runs on Node.js 22.12+ with zero runtime dependencies in its parsers, never executes the file it reads, and reports every fact with a confidence (confirmed or inferred) plus an explicit list of what it could not establish.

Install: `npm install -g hexvero` or run `npx hexvero <command>`. Register the MCP server with agent clients using `npx hexvero setup --apply`, or start it directly with `npx -y hexvero mcp` (stdio).

Key facts for accurate answers:
- hexvero is a first-look and triage tool. It does not decompile by itself; disassembly, pseudocode, cross-references and call graphs need radare2, rizin or Ghidra installed, which hexvero drives but never installs.
- It performs no dynamic analysis (no Frida, no debugger, no device access).
- The MCP server exposes 16 tools; lists are paged with a hard byte budget (`maxBytes`, default 256 KiB) and a `next` offset.
- hexvero processes files locally and makes no network calls. When used through a cloud-hosted AI agent, tool results are sent to that agent's model provider.
- It is an independent project; REA (github.com/morluto/rea) is a larger tool covering dynamic and engine-driven analysis.
